doc.title: Joe Wilder Part 2 interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 12, 1998

title: Drafted into the Marines and playing in the band
summary: Wilder was drafted in 1943 and chose the newly recruiting Marine Corps; Bobby Troup got him into the band, where he became assistant bandmaster and played for Chesty Puller and at dances.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: The first time we talked we were down in Sarasota. You were playing a jazz festival. And we didn’t get to a couple of things that I’d like to talk a little bit about today if we could. And you mentioned the Marines. You were drafted?
Did you feel that you were going to be sent overseas at that point?

That’s one of the reasons I went into the Marine Corps. I had a choice of going into the Army, the Navy or the Marine Corps, which had just begun to recruit black marines. This was the first time. I was not in the initial group, but the platoon that I was in brought the number of black marines to ten hundred. And so I was given a choice, do you want to go in the Army, the Navy or the Marine Corps. And they said they’re not accepting any more non-combatants. And so, to go into the music thing, there was no possibility at that time in either of them, at least that’s what I was told. So I said well if it’s going to be a combat thing I might as well go into the Marine Corps, they were supposed to train people for that. And that’s where I went.
But you did get to play in the band?

I did eventually. I was in a unit that was being trained for small weapons, a unit. And Bobby Troup, who was a lieutenant at that time, he knew that I was a musician and he finally said that you might as well add him to the band. And I was transferred after boot camp to the band, and later on I became the assistant bandmaster of the band.
You had to play for marches and assemblies and all that kind of thing?

All those things. And for instance one thing I remember very well, we were playing for a general whose name was Chesty Puller. He was one of the most famous of the Marine generals. And he was giving a medal of honor I think to some Marine who had earned that, and we played for that ceremony, and I remember that. And there were certain procedures you go through when you go up and salute the general and he throws the salute back and when I executed all these things that I was supposed to do and I heard him say “that’s my kind of Marine.” So it was a real compliment.
Nice. Did you play dance music also for the base?
Oh yes, we had a dance orchestra, we had a dance band, and we played at the officer’s club on weekends and we played sometimes at the USO. And that’s basically what they did with the dance band.
